#5544. The Future of Home: 5 Trends for the Next 50 Years

What does the future of housing design look like? Much like with homes today, trends will be tied to how people live. To predict where design is headed, we need to consider how lifestyles are changing, identify which needs have staying power, and anticipate how homes might evolve to meet them.

DAHLIN Group assembled the top trends for the next 50 years to mark the firm’s 50th anniversary, reflecting on decades of design work to determine what the future looks like. According to DAHLIN, these will be key trends:

BUILDER spoke with DAHLIN’s Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, and Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, for their insight on why these trends will endure.

Fifty years is a long time to forecast residential design trends. How did you decide on these five trends, and what’s behind their staying power?

Wagner: A responsible 50-year view should not claim to know the exact layout, style, or construction method people will use. It should identify what future design must be able to do.

The common principle is agency: giving people more useful choices without requiring them to rebuild their lives or surroundings every time circumstances change.

The solutions to these needs will manifest in dramatically different ways over the next 50 years, but the needs themselves are unlikely to disappear.

How will wellness become more integrated?

Julian: Wellness will move deeper into the core decisions that shape everyday performance.

Daylight, window placement and performance, shading, material choices, air filtration, thermal zoning, and access to outdoor space will be considered together, rather than added as isolated features.

We also expect the idea of restorative space to become more distributed. A home does not need one wellness room if daylight, nature, movement, quiet, and thermal comfort are part of the daily path through the house. That makes wellness more relevant across housing types and price points.

The larger shift is from visible elements to a measurable and felt experience: cleaner air, better control, more useful daylight, a stronger relationship to the outdoors, and spaces that support both activity and retreat.

Design is already leaning away from fully open concept. How might this evolve?

Wagner: People want connection without constant exposure. The open plan still serves cooking, gathering, and shared family life extremely well, but a home now has to absorb more simultaneous activities. A call, homework, quiet conversation, and meal preparation may all happen at once.

People do not necessarily want more rooms; they want more control over how rooms relate.

These allow a space to borrow light and belong to the larger home when open, then become visually or acoustically distinct when needed.

Over time, this can make floor plans less defined. A room may shift between office, study, guest space, care space, or retreat because its boundaries and connections were designed to change.

The goal is not maximum openness at every moment. It is to give the homeowner control over when spaces participate in the life of the home and when they recede.

How will the design partnership with AI evolve?

Wagner: AI can already help teams generate and compare more early visual directions, translate abstract language into discussable imagery, and communicate a concept before investing in a complete visualization package. It can also help align a client and design team when they’re using the same word to mean different things.

The important limitation is that human expertise remains vital in framing the challenge, recognizing what is plausible, selecting the direction that serves the client best, and turning an evocative image into architecture that functions.

AI can quickly generate ideas and multiply options, but the designer must still decide which options deserve to move forward and turn them into a workable, real plan.

The near-term model is therefore collaborative. AI broadens the field of possibilities, while human experts frame the question, curate the outputs, and carry the selected idea into a coherent, buildable design.

Homeowners are placing greater importance on opportunities for social connection. How will future site and community planning support this?

Julian: Instead of relying only on a large destination facility such as a clubhouse or pool area, communities can offer a network of smaller lawns, gardens, play and sport areas, outdoor work settings, cafes or neighborhood retail, and places to sit along daily routes.

Smaller scale can also make participation easier and more approachable. It’s easier to join one of a few seats than to become the only person in a room designed for dozens. The same amount of common area can create more opportunities for connection when it’s placed closer to where people live and is shaped for different levels of participation.

When social space is woven into day-to-day patterns, community becomes a series of low-pressure encounters that can grow into familiarity and belonging.

Why will flexibility be the key to longevity in design?

Julian: Flexibility supports longevity when it reduces the cost and disruption of change. A room that has no assigned use may be flexible on paper, but true adaptability comes from practical decisions: useful daylight, appropriate openings, accessible routes, service relationships, and connections to indoor and outdoor space.

Those decisions determine whether a garage bay can credibly become an office or gym, or whether an ADU can serve a renter, a returning child, or an aging parent at different points in time.

The benefit is not that one design and layout lasts forever. It’s designing change into the bones of the home so that the home can adapt for a wide variety of family configurations without becoming obsolete.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.

#5543. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

#5541. A New Wave of Opportunity Zones Is Coming in 2027—and Home Values Are Already Surging in Key States

The United States has thousands of new Opportunity Zones, a designation that could bring rising values to many emerging housing markets.

The Treasury Department last week announced 6,576 new Opportunity Zones (OZ), which will maintain that status for the next decade. All 50 states and the District of Columbia have zones in the mix, and 2,594 of them are in rural areas. OZs benefit from enhanced economic incentives, and they're targeted at communities with the potential to grow.

“By designating thousands of new Qualified Opportunity Zones, the IRS and Treasury are enabling targeted investment and growth in communities where it is needed the most," IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.

This is the second round of OZs since the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act established the program in 2017. The private sector has invested $110 billion in developing the first crop, Treasury said. The original OZs remain active through 2028, and the new ones begin in 2027. Some OZs were renewed.

States submitted nominations from about 25,300 census tracts eligible for the program, and leaders cheered their wins. There are about 25% fewer tracts than last time.

"Whether it's bringing new life to a downtown, creating great-paying jobs, or building housing for more families, these Opportunity Zones will help attract investments that can make a real difference in the lives of Ohioans," Gov. Mike DeWine said of Ohio's 260 new OZs.

“Virginia is ready to harness the potential of Opportunity Zones,” Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger said of the state's 153 new OZs. “I worked closely with local leaders across Virginia to make sure we supported the priorities that mattered most to local communities."

Property data group ATTOM analyzed 3,805 OZ census tracts from the last tranche and found median single-family home and condo prices rose in 48.1% them. Compare that to home prices outside of OZs, which rose 51.6%.

Some OZs see their home values rise much more quickly. ATTOM found that about 9.4% of the OZ census tracts saw their highest median home value since the Great Recession in the third quarter of 2026. About 27.1% of them saw double-digit growth in home values year over year.

“Opportunity Zones remain a notably lower-cost segment of the housing market, with nearly 80% of these areas posting median home prices below the national median,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Even so, home values were only slightly less likely to rise in these areas in the third quarter, suggesting that many of these communities are still moving broadly with the market.”

As far as states with a lot of OZ price growth, Maine came in first, with 64% of its OZs seeing median home prices rise. South Carolina (61.3%), Wisconsin (58.3%), Virginia (53%), and Oregon (52.3%) rounded out the top five.

ATTOM noted that many of the census tracts recorded a low number of sales, so the data can be volatile. Still, 79.5% of them had home prices below the national median. Outside of them, just 50.4% of tracts had prices below the national median.

Michael Tillman, CEO of OZ developer PTM Partners, tells Realtor.com® the program also gives developers time to experiment. His company builds workforce housing in Florida using cold-formed steel and vertical integration.

"These are not build-and-flip products; we want to be there as their family grows," Tillman said of the units. "That's stickier than high-end luxury. There's got to be more institutional capital with that long-term focus."

OZs tend to have higher poverty rates, lower median family income, and more housing cost burdens than a typical area. Some are in urban areas, and others are in rural ones.

Brookings Institute analyzed the OZ program and found half of the zones saw "accelerated growth." But it said the designation alone doesn't create success. Local market conditions and state and local regulations play a role. And, while they do often mean new investment, that can vary depending on the development already there.

"Investment alone is not synonymous with shared prosperity," Brookings said in the report. "In some places, OZ capital has expanded housing supply, supported business formation, created jobs, and leveraged underutilized community assets—while in others, it flowed toward projects with limited community benefits or into neighborhoods already on a growth path."

Brookings also noted the first round of OZs came when the country already saw increased building. What this means in the current, challenged market has yet to be seen. States should develop a strategy for how to develop each zone.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5540. Google Cloud takes aim at the cost of keeping idle AI agents running on Kubernetes

Kubernetes has become the go-to platform for distributed training and inference, but what happens to the compute bill when it runs AI agents that spend most of their time waiting?

When an agent’s container or virtual machine stays provisioned, customers pay for the wait as well as the work. To help customers control those costs and make agent workloads more predictable, Google LLC has donated three projects to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, according to Allan Naim (pictured, left), director of product management, AI infrastructure, at Google Cloud. For Kubernetes itself, the new challenge is freeing up compute between bursts of activity while letting each agent pick up where it left off.

“Act 2 is a few years back; Kubernetes became the de facto for inference and training,” Naim said. “What’s really interesting right now is we’re embarking on this Act 3 … where the typical patterns are very, very different from how Kubernetes was designed.”

Naim and Gari Singh (right), product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google Cloud is using open-source tools to cut compute costs when AI agents sit idle. (* Disclosure below.)

Cost presents a serious problem in agentic workloads, with agents sitting idle 90% to 95% of the time waiting on models, test runs or human approvals, Naim explained. Google developed Agent Substrate, an open-source runtime that hosts AI agents in isolated environments on Kubernetes. When an agent is suspended, the runtime saves a snapshot of its memory and local files and frees up its compute for other agents. When work resumes, it restores the agent from that snapshot in an available sandbox.

“It helps from an economic standpoint,” Naim said. “We’ve seen 10x reduction in cost in terms of running Agent Substrate on Kubernetes versus running these agents directly on dedicated virtual machines and containers.”

Security is another concern. In response, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018, which sits on top of the host kernel to block or audit every system call an agent makes, according to Singh.

“Agents and agent harnesses are designed to solve a problem — and to try to solve a problem — until they can’t solve the problem,” Singh said. “They will find all kinds of clever workarounds. They know everything that’s around. You want to make sure that it didn’t go make some low-level change to [your] low-level security, didn’t make an outbound network call, didn’t try to open a file that it shouldn’t.”

Google is also working with Anyscale Inc. on KubeRay, which runs Anyscale’s Ray platform natively on Kubernetes so platform teams can offer distributed training and inference to many research groups, Singh noted. OpenRL brings that approach to reinforcement learning, which teaches post-trained models guardrails, Naim added.

“In the past, to do reinforcement learning, you needed to hire a dozen research scientists with PhDs,” Naim said. “Our goal was, ‘How can we bring reinforcement learning into the world of platform engineering so that you can run reinforcement learning on your Kubernetes environment and take advantage of it to actually do continuous improvement for your agentic workload?'”

#5539. Inside the $3.25 Million Pasadena Glass Pavilion That’s Still Studied in Architecture Classes Today

A three-bedroom midcentury modern home designed by Case Study architect Craig Ellwood has just come on the market in Pasadena, CA, for $3.25 million. It features a notable cantilevered glass pavilion.

Built in 1965, the Kubly House was originally constructed for less than $45,000. The 2,227-square-foot home has since been thoughtfully updated.

“What makes this house special is its architecture and design, and how true it has remained to the original,” says Chris Suarez, who is co-listing the property with Kimberly Benz of Suarez + Benz at Compass. “Nothing was significantly altered. Everything done was intended to restore the house to its original condition. The footprint, the floors, the glass—everything has remained true to the original design.”

Located in the Linda Vista neighborhood, the home has an iconic redwood, cantilevered glass pavilion that opens to a single-level floor plan. The private half-acre lot includes a pool and spa surrounded by lush landscaping with eucalyptus and oak trees.

With exposed post-and-beam construction, clean horizontal lines, and expansive walls of glass, the home was designed to give the illusion of floating above its natural surroundings. The deck was recently restored using specially milled wood.

“It was sourced from northern Washington and brought down here,” Suarez notes. “Everything was done painstakingly to avoid altering the house’s integrity, architecture, and design. That being said, significant work has been done, including updates to the roof, infrastructure, air conditioning, and electrical systems. All the major systems have been updated, but you wouldn’t necessarily know it because the work was done so carefully.”

Originally commissioned by ArtCenter College of Design alumni and educators Don and Sally Kubly, the home represents their understanding of design and the culture of the college community. It is still studied in classes there.

“Don was ArtCenter’s first president in Pasadena,” Suarez explains. “There’s also a connection through Craig Ellwood, who designed ArtCenter’s main campus building. The main campus is an incredible steel-and-glass building designed by Ellwood. Don played a significant role in moving the school from Los Angeles to Pasadena, where he served as president for many years. He’s very well known within that community, and this house is significant to the college’s history and culture.”

Based on available architectural records, the Kubly House is said to be Ellwood’s only documented residential project in Pasadena.

After remaining in the Kubly family for nearly six decades, the home changed hands for $3.6 million in 2022. Since then, the sellers have undertaken a preservation-minded restoration with Carl Bronson of Bronstruction, updating major systems to contemporary standards.

“A house that helped usher in much midcentury modernism was the Glass House, designed by Philip Johnson around 1948 or 1949,” Benz notes. “That design was definitely something Ellwood loved. You can clearly see that house’s influence here, which is important because it reveals some of the influences behind Ellwood’s work.”

Benz adds that the home’s design was also influenced by Ellwood’s peers, including midcentury designer George Nelson.

“A furniture plan developed for the house clearly referenced Mies van der Rohe and George Nelson, both important figures in midcentury modern design,” she says. “Even the deck and the steps leading to the house resemble a George Nelson bench. There’s actually a bench built into the concrete wall near the pool that resembles a George Nelson design. I don’t know whether Nelson designed or made it, but the influence is certainly there.”

The house is special because many of the original details have remained intact, she adds.

“You can see the influence of the people Ellwood admired throughout the house,” Benz says. “That significance is what makes this house important when you look at the midcentury modernist movement. All these examples are visible in the house and remain there.”

Some of the built-in furniture has a distinctive style, too.

“There’s a stunning floating credenza that looks like a George Nelson piece,” she notes. “We think it might be one of his designs. It’s in the living room. There’s also a built-in console that might be a George Nelson design as well. So, some of the furniture is actually built into the architecture.”

While some pieces are originals and others are reproductions, Benz says, “the most important thing was following the original plan. The history of this house is everything.”

When staging the home, she says they were “fortunate to discover an original interior design study among the blueprints, plans, and documents that came with the house. We were able to look at that study, and it became a guide and a road map for staging the property. Sourcing the furniture was a challenge because we had to find the specific pieces.”

The city of Pasadena has also identified the property as eligible for individual listing on the National Register of Historic Places.

#5537. Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.11% Rate

Mortgage rates continued their slow retreat for a fourth consecutive week, mirroring the trajectory of bond yields, although this week's hotter-than-expected inflation print suggests the relief will be short-lived.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans decreased to 7.11% for the week ending Nov. 12, down 7 basis points from 7.18% the week before, according to Freddie Mac. Even with this steady month-long decline, borrowing costs remain significantly higher than they were a year ago, when rates averaged 6.24% during the same period in 2025.

So what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

At today's 7.11% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,314. This reflects a $16 monthly reduction from the previous week’s payment of $2,330.

Compared to the 6.24% average from November 2025, which required a $2,116 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $198 more every single month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.11% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,791.

This reflects a $20 decrease from last week's monthly cost of $2,811. Compared to the 6.24% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,552, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $239 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $193 in relative relief.

The long-term financial picture shows how this continued downward drift improves overall borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.11% rate will pay a total of $833,080 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage. While current financing costs remain elevated compared to year-ago levels, this total still represents a distinct contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630.

By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $57,550 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.11% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,004,902 for principal and interest. If that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $69,421 for FHA buyers.

While stubborn inflation may limit how much further rates can fall in the weeks ahead, this four-week pullback has helped trim monthly expenses for buyers jumping in the late-fall market.

Not only do these unique properties offer a place to call home but they also provide a chance to preserve a piece of the past while creating something entirely your own.

Full of charm, character, and possibilities, these structures feature many original details, including vintage bank vaults and architectural details.

From Maine to Wisconsin, we found five converted banks and schoolhouses priced below $400,000 that offer a unique opportunity to live somewhere with a story to tell.

CSAA Landmark Schoolhouse: Built in 1865, this 600-square-foot building has been converted into a stylish one-bedroom, loft-style home.

The charming open floor plan has hardwood floors and a cozy living room that flows into the dining area and kitchen. A spiral staircase leads to the sleeping quarters, which have vaulted wood ceilings. Recent improvements include energy-efficient hydronic baseboard heating.

A garden, an oversized shed, and a hot tub are also on the wooded lot.

Michele M. Barry of Lake Lady Property Management is the listing agent.

Former Stayton School: Set on 3 acres, this 4,000-square-foot building has 1,400 square feet of finished living space. It comes with unfinished space for the next buyer to remodel.

Built in 1946, the home features many original details, including preserved hardwood floors, custom millwork, oversized windows, and high ceilings. The living room still has a chalkboard lining the wall, and wall-mounted water fountains nod to the building’s past. The updated kitchen has custom cabinetry and a farmhouse sink. An original raised “performance stage” could be used for entertaining or converted into a studio.

Former Stockton Springs High School: Built in 1880, this 6,244-square-foot former schoolhouse serves as a blank canvas. It could be transformed into a one-of-a-kind residence, a multipurpose retreat, or an event space.

The generously sized rooms offer endless possibilities for entertaining, workshops, gatherings, or other uses (subject to town approval). #5535. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

#5534. Report: Demand Surges for Single-Family Rentals

Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month.

“For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.”

The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise.

Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs, according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report.

In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down.

Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals.

Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%.

Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%).

#5533. Agents idling while they wait on humans push Kubernetes to hand back unused resources

Agentic AI workloads are handing Kubernetes an unexpected second act. The orchestrator once dismissed as reliable but boring is now at the center of how enterprises plan to run autonomous software.

Past platform shifts, from physical servers to virtual machines and from virtual machines to containers, forced companies to wipe the slate clean and start over. This shift is different because Kubernetes was built as a platform for building platforms, according to Bobby Allen (pictured), cloud therapist at Google Cloud LLC.

“Kubernetes now, 11, 12+ years in, has this whole new life,” Allen said. “You don’t need a new platform this time. … This shift doesn’t mean that you’ve got to retool and rebuild and replatform everything, and I think that could be comforting for folks to realize that they don’t have to start from scratch.”

Allen spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Kubernetes is recovering resources spent on idle agentic AI workloads. (* Disclosure below.)

Google is putting that view into practice. The company has donated Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, while engineering teams are tuning Kubernetes for agents rather than building a new stack.

“Google is doubling down on our commitment to not just open source but community-driven, collaborative, multiple-partner-involvement open source,” Allen said. “These concepts are foundational, but they’re important enough that we need to all contribute and shape these together.”

Efficiency is a big part of the motivation. Agents spend long stretches idle while they wait for human input, and the projects aim to give those resources back during the downtime, Allen explained.

“These are kind of different efforts that contribute to an open, flexible, transparent, collaborative way to make agentic workloads run better so that we can have these amazing outcomes but also be efficient with our resources,” Allen said. “We don’t want to have this sci-fi Star Trek moment where we’re stepping into the future and kill the planet.”

#5532. Detached Home in Desirable DC Neighborhood Gets Major Discount—and the Photos Hide a Wild Catch

A Washington, DC, home has been put on the market for far under the area’s median listing price, but the reason is buried within the listing—and online forums are not happy about it.

At first glance, 1007 Evarts St NE is a stunning six-bed, five-bath home, with a jaw dropping $375,000 price tag, nearly 40% below the zip code’s median listing price of $607,500.

The first nine photos on the listing show an updated, bright, and beautifully staged home with a perfectly manicured lawn. But flip to the tenth photo, and the image changes. The rest of the photos show a smaller home, stripped to the studs and in need of complete rehabilitation, both inside and out.

The key detail then becomes clear: a watermark reading “Architect’s rendering—not an actual photo” in the corner of the listing’s primary photos.

The property details tell the rest of the story.

“Much of the pre-construction work is already done. Demolition is complete and the structure is down to a clean shell with the framing exposed,” the property details read. “The sale includes a DC-approved plan set for a full rebuild. The renderings in the photos show the finished home as designed.”

Investors, developers, and 203(k) rehab buyers who want to skip design stage and jump right into construction are the ideal buyers, according to the listing.

With that information taken into consideration, the severe price reduction from the area’s norm listing makes sense.

However, the listing has still received heat online, where one Threads user reposted the images with the caption, “This has got to be the most click bait home ive ever seen…..this gotta be illegal, right?”

The replies are filled with equally outraged users.

“Is that AI renderings of potential build and then the actual pics of an as-is shack???” wrote another user.

“The listing is deceptive because you don’t know what you’re looking at. I certainly don’t. And you’re right, you can’t advertise potential. It’s absolutely unethical,” wrote one user, who identified herself as a real estate agent. “The architect rendered pics should have never been included. Those would easily be shown separately to a potential buyer. If you’re selling a clean shell, that’s all that should be pictured.”

The listing did have one defender in the replies: the home’s listing agent, Tohmai Smith. He argued that all of the necessary information is available in the listing, and if he was trying to deceive buyers, pictures of the house as-is wouldn’t have been included.

“It’s in the description: ‘The renderings in the photos show the finished home as designed.’ And they’re not AI. A licenses architect built them from the DC-approved plans, which convey with the sale,” Smith wrote. “The finished home is a $1.3M house. The $400K buys you the shell, the approved plans and a head start.”

Users continued to question his claim that the photos weren’t made with AI, pointing out discrepancies in the rendered photos and structural issues with the back staircase as potential clues that they weren’t made with professional architectural programs.

Others questioned the possibility of fitting a six-bed, five-bath home on the moderate 5,066-square-foot lot.

In subsequent replies, Smith explained the use of 203(k) loans to both buy a home and finance the renovation in one mortgage and further argued that the purpose of the renderings is to show buyers the home’s potential. Within these posts, he invited interested parties or those with questions to send him a direct message.

“Without these renderings, how would a buyer know what’s possible? Even after seeing them, people can’t believe it,” Smith wrote. “But it IS possible, and that’s exactly why I show them.”

Bright MLS, which is responsible for listings in the Mid-Atlantic region and carries the Evarts Street listing, has a rule that any “Virtually Staged” images must be labeled, and no AI alterations can alter permanent features or hide defects, according to Imagen for Real Estate.

Another law has been proposed in Washington DC to require listings to disclose any photo editing and include both unedited photos and a written list of all changes.

Despite online controversy, the listing for 1007 Evarts Street NE appears to follow both the active and proposed guidelines, by including actual photos of the property and describing the state of the home in the property details section.

Realtor.com reached out to both Smith and Bright MLS for comments on the use of renderings in listings, but received no response at the time of publication.

#5531. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5530. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5529. Grand Rapids, MI Struggles with Low Starter Home Availability Compared to Other Cities

For many prospective homeowners, the dream of a starter home has felt increasingly out of reach. Rising prices and climbing mortgage rates have compounded the challenge, making affordable options feel scarce.

Economists at Realtor.com® found that nationally, the share of starter homes in active inventory fell from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. During that same period, starter home prices rose by 30.8%, from approximately $260,000 to $340,000.

In Grand Rapids, MI, the market has followed this trend, experiencing a downturn in available starter homes in recent years.

A starter home is typically defined as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price, making it more accessible for a first-time buyer or a household with an income at or below the area median. These homes are generally smaller and offer a lower-cost entry into homeownership, improving housing affordability.

In Grand Rapids, the share of starter homes was 32.8% in 2019 and remained steady at 32.8% in 2022. However, by 2026, that share had decreased to 31.4%.

This represents a 1.4 point change decline since 2019, reflecting a tightening market for entry-level buyers in the area.

Among the other Midwestern metropolitan areas tracked, Grand Rapids ranked near the bottom with a 2026 starter home share of 31.4%, outpacing only Madison, WI at 29.4%.

By comparison, the highest overall starter share in 2026 belongs to affordable Midwest and Rust Belt metros: Toledo, OH (42.1%), St. Louis, MO (40.7%), and Detroit, MI (39.8%).

#5528. Quarterback Sam Hartman is ‘The Bachelor’ Season 30’s Leading Man—Marking the First Return to Bachelor Mansion Post-Renovation

Washington Commanders quarterback Sam Hartman is packing his bags for Bachelor Mansion.

The 27-year-old Charlotte, NC native has been announced as the “leading man” for Season 30 of “The Bachelor.”

A statement from ABC Entertainment says the “pro athlete is ready to find his forever teammate,” and will use “the same leadership and heart that won over fans on the field” as he prepares to hand out roses to the women vying for his love—and a Neil Lane engagement ring.

Hartman’s official “Bachelor” bio notes that he’s a “standout alum of Wake Forest and Notre Dame, where set legendary ACC records, including most career touchdown passes and 300-yard passing games.”

It’s not the heartthrob’s first time on television, as he was also a fan-favorite in the Netflix documentary series, “QB1: Beyond the Lights,” where he shared his journey as a top high school senior quarterback before moving into his Division I collegiate career.

“I’m very nervous,” Hartman admitted during a Nov. 13 appearance on “Good Morning America.”

“I have a tough time holding a conversation with one girl,” he said. “30 is gonna be pretty tough.”

Hartman said the experience felt too great to pass on, and sounds ready to head down the aisle with one of the 30 contestants he’ll soon meet.

“I think anybody in their right mind, if you get told, ‘Hey, you get a chance to go find the love of your life,’ I know one thing: When people are saying ‘I do,’ they don’t ask you where you met, they just ask you if you want to do it forever. And I don’t see any problem with that.”

Hartman split his high school career between two private schools in North Carolina and South Carolina. Although his football career has taken him across the country, his parents reside in Mount Pleasant, SC, where his father coaches high school football—a gig that’s kept him busy for more than two decades.

It’s a shame that the show’s milestone episode sees the lead heading to the hometowns of the final four contestants, and not vice versa, as Mount Pleasant is certainly a lovely place to visit. The suburban town is located just outside of Charleston, across the Cooper River.

Still, Hartman has his parents’ unrelenting support.

“They’re excited. My mom and I have a really cool relationship, and my pops is supportive,” he said. “Their big thing is to just be myself and enjoy the experience and trust your instincts, trust your gut. That’s what’s gotten you so far.”

While most of what lies ahead for Season 30 of “The Bachelor” remains a mystery, it’s safe to assume viewers can count on one thing: a return to Bachelor Mansion.

The show’s been on a two-year hiatus, so it’s been quite some time since we’ve seen a regular season set within the walls of the franchise’s most iconic property.

Built in 2004 by contractor Marshall Haraden, who still owns it today, the Bachelor Mansion’s real name is Villa de Vina. It’s a 9,000-square-foot estate where Haraden and his family reside for most of the year, but move out and stay in a hotel when the series is in production.

Each season, crews clear out much of the family’s furniture and redecorate to transform their abode into the backdrop fans have grown to love over countless seasons.

Although the lavish home has become an iconic destination in its own right, contestants have historically complained about the cramped living quarters they endure for the six weeks the show is in production.

Cast members famously sleep in bunk beds arranged in rows, and share crowded bathrooms and limited storage space.

Earlier this year, a dozen beloved Bachelor Nation alumni—including “The Bachelorette” Season 15 runner-up Tyler Cameron and former “The Bachelorette” lead Tayshia Adams—competed in an HGTV makeover competition called “Bachelor Mansion Takeover.”

“I did still have PTSD walking in here because I haven’t been here in years,” Adams admitted in an Entertainment Tonight interview ahead of the series premiere. Still, the cast seemed proud of the improvements they made to the home, which included upgraded bunk beds that Adams shared were “ten times better” than the previous setup.

“The Bachelor” Season 30 premieres Sunday, March 21 at 8:00 p.m. EST/PST on ABC.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5526. Greenville, SC, Struggles With Low Starter Home Availability Compared to Other Cities

In a recent metro-by-metro analysis, Realtor.com® examined the state of the American starter home. For many would-be buyers, these entry-level homes have felt increasingly scarce as rising prices and climbing mortgage rates create significant financial hurdles.

Furthermore, research supports this feeling of a shrinking market. The national share of starter homes in active inventory fell from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. During that same period, starter home prices rose 30.8%, from approximately $260,000 to $340,000.

In Greenville, SC, the market has experienced a downturn in starter home availability in recent years.

A starter home is defined as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price, making it an accessible option for a first-time buyer or a household with an Income at or below the area median. These homes are typically smaller and offer a more manageable entry point into homeownership, boosting overall market affordability.

In the Greenville-Anderson-Greer, SC, metro area, the share of starter homes was 32.2% in 2019. This figure fell to 26.6% in 2022 before recovering slightly to 31.3% in 2026.

However, this still represents a -0.9 point change since 2019, indicating a slight tightening of the market for entry-level buyers.

Greenville trailed neighboring South Carolina and Georgia markets like Charleston (36.7%), Augusta (35.1%), and Columbia (34.7%) in starter home inventory.

However, between 2019 and 2026, Greenville experienced a relatively mild drop of just 0.9 percentage points, reaching a 2026 starter home share of 31.3%. This stability allowed Greenville to pull ahead of nearby regional peers that suffered steep losses over the same period, including Columbia (-8.3 points to 26.4%) and Augusta (-6.5 points to 28.6%).

After dipping to 26.6% in 2022, Greenville rebounded strongly by 2026, nearly matching Charleston, which saw its share contract by 5.0 percentage points to 31.7%.

By 2026, Greenville’s 31.3% starter home share closely aligns with major adjacent hubs like Atlanta (31.5%) and Charlotte (31.1%), though Charlotte achieved a 1.0 point gain while Atlanta fell by 3.3 points.

#5525. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure shakes AI industry’s foundations

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

Honeypot or not, the Chinese executive/accused spy with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted an affair this week should have been a flashing red light to him. So should fraternizing with one of your own VPs — and reportedly another employee too!

In the end, all that, and maybe more to come, was just too much for Nvidia’s board to bear despite the commanding position Huang (pictured) held not only at Nvidia but in the entire artificial intelligence industry. Indeed, the speed with which he resigned — spectacularly stupid as his behavior was — still makes me wonder if there are other shoes to drop, especially on the legal or national security fronts. Market researcher SemiAnalysis thinks it came down to pressure from the U.S. intelligence community that’s very unhappy Nvidia chips have apparently been smuggled to China.

Huang was something of an AI puppet master, providing the chips and software to power the entire industry as well as seemingly unlimited cash to fund and backstop everyone from AI leaders such as OpenAI and Anthropic to innumerable cloud compute providers worldwide. No single person inside or outside Nvidia seems likely to fill that role.

However, Nvidia really is much more than Jensen Huang. Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress helped craft the financial arrangements that in part put Nvidia at the center of AI — though for what it’s worth, Huang himself wasn’t a fan lately. Some of his direct reports such as high-performance computing chief Ian Buck seem quite capable of carrying on, if perhaps not with Huang’s panache. One company is never one person, and shouldn’t be. I expect a less centralized Nvidia going forward, whoever’s at the top.

More than that, AI is much more than Jensen Huang, and it will continue to be going forward. It’s easy to forget that although Huang brilliantly helped create this new wave, AI and its enablers also are what made him a rock star. But that time is now over. Nvidia and certainly the AI industry shouldn’t be depending on one person to keep everything afloat anyway.

The reverberations of his sudden and shocking departure will continue to echo for a long time to come across Nvidia, its investors watching hundreds of billions of market cap evaporate, legions of Jensen fanboys and the entire artificial intelligence ecosystem. A lot of people are hoping desperately that he didn’t just pop the AI bubble (though others are hoping he did). It seems unlikely this will be the pin, but we’re dealing with a lot of unlikely things in the past week or so, for better and worse, and this shock is clearly rattling the foundations.

All that managed to overshadow what otherwise would be the big news this week: Anthropic went on the road to pitch its initial public offering. It’s hoping to raise more than $64 billion and keep the AI trade humming in Nvidia’s near-term absence. Looks like next Thursday is the big day.

And it’s not the only good news in AI — that is, if the IPO is successful. After a difficult month on the stock front, uber neocloud CoreWeave provided a pleasant AI surprise with upside earnings and guidance, lifting its shares almost 25% Wednesday. AI chipmaker Cerebras’ shares rose almost 18% in late trading Thursday on positive guidance and a Microsoft deal. Cisco Systems said demand is strong for AI infrastructure, even if investors shrugged, and chipmaking equipment supplier Applied Materials said AI boosted demand as well.

Not everyone fared so well, though. Dutch neocloud Nebius saw its shares drop almost 17% Thursday as it lowered its outlook despite close to sevenfold revenue growth in the last quarter. The stock drop no doubt was partly because of Nvidia, which is, of course, an investor. CoreWeave –yes, another Nvidia investment — lost 7% Thursday.

Couple of really big outages out there: first, Microsoft Outlook, grounding a lot of office workers, then the whole damn U.S. air traffic control system, grounding thousands of flights.

Sovereignty is on many enterprise buyers’ lips these days, the notion that enterprises need a way to assert more control over their technology estates and protect their customers’ data. TheCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin just completed the first of a series of reports on how to approach sovereignty, this one focused on the hyperscale cloud providers.

The software orchestrator Kubernetes has become boring, but as SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier said at this week’s KubeCon in Salt Lake City, that means it’s a success — with lessons for AI developers. “A lot of things that are happening in cloud-native that were involved in microservices in Kubernetes world are actually the same challenges in the AI world,” he noted.

IBM has been working hard on quantum computing for a long time now, but at its Quantum Developer Conference in Chicago this week, it showed significant progress, according to Dave Vellante. Its goal now is to show actual industry impact by 2028, a laudable goal that presents a lot of challenges, Dave wrote in his Special Breaking Analysis this week.

Next week the SC26 high-performance computing conference comes to Chicago, and theCUBE and theCUBE Research will be onsite with interviews and analysis. There’s also Microsoft Ignite in San Francisco. And earnings next week include… Nvidia! Bring the popcorn.

Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, most of it not salacious, along with analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:

Dario goes overboard with AI claims ahead of Anthropic’s IPO — the same guy who says AI could also extinguish us. Somebody give him back his Xanax! Also, I really don’t think mental illness is a compute problem.

Gartner forecasts AI infrastructure spending to represent 59% of total global AI spending in 2027

Gartner also forecasts AI will drive a net increase of 1.7M jobs by 2030 That one number hides a lot of job losses and especially job “transformations,” and not to throw shade on Gartner in particular, anyone betting on AI’s impact out in 2030 is barely more than guessing.

United Airlines is banning AI bots from booking flights, following Amazon and Walmart doing the same thing for shopping. Aren’t travel and shopping a prime use case for AI agents? But they’re still trying: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its ‘dots’ AI agents to make purchases for users.

Getting too close to Trump was a mistake, says Nick Clegg. Amen. We’ve already seen them trying to backpedal, starting with Palantir CEO Alex Karp, who had the audacity to call his company “progressive.” Dude, sit down.

#5524. Indianapolis, IN Struggles with Low Starter Home Availability Compared to Other Cities

For many prospective homeowners, the dream of purchasing a first home can feel increasingly out of reach. A recent analysis by Realtor.com® explores the availability of starter home options across the country, revealing a challenging landscape for many would-be buyers.

Nationally, the share of starter homes in active inventory has seen a decline, falling from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. This scarcity is compounded by rising prices and climbing mortgage rates. Over the same period, starter home prices increased by 30.8%, from approximately $260,000 to $340,000.

In Indianapolis, IN, the market reflects this national trend, with the availability of starter homes experiencing a downturn in recent years. This shift presents new hurdles for those looking to enter the housing market in the area.

A starter home is defined as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price, making it a more accessible option for a first-time buyer. These homes are typically smaller and less expensive, aligning with the budget of a household earning at or below the area's median Income and offering a gateway to homeownership and improved affordability.

In Indianapolis, the share of starter homes has decreased over the past several years. The market saw its starter home share at 36.2% in 2019, which slightly decreased to 35.9% in 2022.

By 2026, the share of starter homes in Indianapolis had fallen to 33.0%. This represents a 3.2 point change since 2019, highlighting a growing challenge for buyers seeking entry-level properties in the metro area.

For those weighing the decision between renting or buying, current data suggests that renting may be the more financially prudent choice for now. According to the Realtor.com® July Rent Report, the cost of buying a starter home was $858 higher per month than renting one across the 50 largest metros.

In fact, renting is the more affordable option in all 50 of the largest U.S. metros, allowing renters to save money that could be put toward a future down payment. A rent vs. buy calculator can help individuals assess their specific financial situation.

In the Indianapolis, IN, market, the median rent for an apartment was $1,273 as of July 2026. This represents a 1.60% decrease year-over-year, making renting an even more attractive option for residents.
