#5523. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. He previously led research on responsible AI at Freddie Mac, and also worked at Meta and the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

Szu Yu Chen is a senior data visualization designer and developer who creates interactive graphics and data-driven experiences. Previously, she worked as a graphics reporter at The Washington Post and the Los Angeles Times.

#5522. Jackson, MS Struggles with Low Starter Home Availability Compared to Other Cities

For many prospective homeowners, the search for an affordable starter home can feel like a daunting task. A recent analysis by Realtor.com® explores the changing landscape of entry-level housing across the country, revealing where these crucial properties are becoming more or less common.

Nationally, starter home options have felt increasingly scarce as rising prices and climbing mortgage rates compound the challenge. According to research, the national share of starter homes in active inventory fell from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. Moreover, during that same period, starter home prices rose 30.8%, from roughly $260,000 to $340,000.

As a result, some markets have seen a significant shift in their housing stock.

In Jackson, MS, the availability of starter homes has experienced a slight downturn in recent years, reflecting the broader challenges facing many homebuyers.

A starter home is defined by Realtor.com as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price, which captures the relative affordability of the lower end of each local market. These homes are typically smaller and less expensive, making them accessible to a first-time buyer or a household with an income at or below the area median.

In Jackson, the share of starter homes was 36.4% in 2019 and rose to 38.6% in 2022. However, by 2026, the share had decreased to 36.3% of the market's available inventory.

Therefore, this represents a -0.1 point change between 2019 and 2026. This slight decline indicates a modest tightening of the market for entry-level buyers in the Jackson area over the past several years.

As Jackson holds a projected 2026 starter home share of 36.3%, it ranks second among neighboring Southern metropolitan areas, trailing only Memphis, TN at 39.2%.

Between 2019 and 2026, Jackson's starter home share showed notable resilience,despite a slight net loss of 0.1 percentage points. This near-zero shift contrasts with neighboring Birmingham, AL and Little Rock, AR, which experienced larger reductions of 2.1 and 1.6 percentage points over the same period, bringing their 2026 shares down to 36.2% and 35.6%, respectively.

In nearby Louisiana, New Orleans suffered a steep drop of 4.4 percentage points to 32.2%, while Baton Rouge contracted by 0.4 percentage points to finish at 32.4%.

Finally, Tennessee neighbors displayed divergent trends, with Knoxville declining by 4.9 percentage points to 31.8% while Nashville-Davidson gained 1.2 percentage points to reach 32.7%.

#5521. Compass Sues 15 MLSs in 8 States Over Marketing Restrictions

As the next heated step in its nationwide battle against MLS incumbents, Compass filed more than a dozen federal antitrust lawsuits against 15 MLSs today, carrying out a promised threat to take a bitter, long-running dispute over restrictions on off-MLS marketing to the courtroom.

According to a release, Compass is accusing the MLSs in question of “fining and punishing agents who publicly market homes as their clients have lawfully instructed.” It also notes that said fines can reach up to $15,000.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson stated. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

One of the initial complaints obtained by RISMedia targets Hive MLS in North Carolina. The 45-page lawsuit alleges two violations of federal antitrust laws, accusing the MLS of conspiracy and an illegal group boycott.

“Homeowners should be free to choose how to sell their own homes without having a competition-killing real estate industry organization tell them how to do it,” the complaint begins.

The lawsuits are against six MLSs based in California:

And six MLSs are spread throughout the country:

Several of the MLSs targeted—including Hive MLS, ARMLS, REcolorado, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS and bridgeMLS—already sued Compass, asking a judge to preemptively declare their rules do not violate antitrust laws. They have characterized their various policies, which restrict how members can market listing off-MLS, as pro-competitive and pro-consumer, and claimed Compass is merely seeking to use its exclusive listings as a “competitive weapon.”

Compass, on the other hand, has repeatedly accused these MLSs of fighting purely to protect their own interests and claimed the MLS industry has long endured antitrust scrutiny from government regulators. It sent letters to many of these MLSs back in September, explicitly threatening to sue and force them to bear the legal costs if they continued enforcing the policies in question.

“It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true,” the Compass spokesperson said. “For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?”

Specifically, the lawsuit targeting Hive mentions restrictions on showings for “Coming Soon” properties and focuses on governance, describing the MLS as a “contract, combination, or conspiracy of competing agents and brokers.” It also points to Hive’s alleged licensing of data to third parties, something Compass has previously criticized.

“MLSs that are comprised of or governed by brokerages and agents with traditional business models have a strong financial incentive to impair the business models of innovators and mavericks who seek to offer marketing options to homeowners that eschew immediate and automatic sharing of their listings on the MLS regardless of the circumstances or preferences of the homeowner,” the lawsuit says.

Other lawsuits viewed by RISMedia, including complaints against San Diego MLS and REcolorado, appeared to be largely similar, though they incorporated at least some unique elements (for instance, the San Diego MLS suit quotes California law as imparting a fiduciary duty of “utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty” on agents, and notes that the Realtor® associations that previously owned REcolorado specifically cited worries about antitrust scrutiny when they sold the MLS to a private company back in 2024).

The lawsuits were filed right on the heels of Compass’ new Broker-to-Broker Cooperation Policy, which requires all Compass agents to cooperate with other brokers and agents unless otherwise instructed by the client in writing. Compass agents must also adhere to the policy when dealing with listings earmarked as Private Exclusives or Coming Soons.

Compass’ arguments against the 15 MLSs echo closely to the brokerage’s complaint in the ongoing lawsuit against the California Regional Multiple Listing Service (CRMLS), which it sued in mid-October.

Prior to Compass’ complaint, CRMLS took the initiative and sued the brokerage in early October. As outlined in its original complaint, CRMLS is asking a federal judge in New York to declare that the organization’s rules do not violate state and federal antitrust laws.

“The Cooperation Rules are straightforward: they require that when a broker publicly markets a property for sale—that property must also be submitted to the MLS for cooperation with other participating brokers,” CRMLS’ original complaint states. “What the rules do not permit is having it both ways—publicly marketing a property to attract buyers while simultaneously withholding that property from the MLS cooperative and the thousands of other brokers and their buyer clients.”

Compass, meanwhile, alleged that CRMLS’ rules were “illegal” and accused the organization of blocking the brokerage’s “better home marketing product to protect Compass’ competitors from having to compete,” in Compass’ original complaint against CRMLS.

“Instead of fixing its anticompetitive rules, CRMLS has escalated enforcement against Compass: by CRMLS’s own count, roughly a quarter of the CRMLS fines for public marketing in 2026 involve Compass listings,” Compass’ complaint continued.

Since then, several other MLSs have joined CRMLS in their lawsuit, or have filed their own against the mega-brokerage. OneKey MLS joined CRMLS in its legal battle late last month, while Texas-based Unlock MLS released its own letter alleging that Compass had mischaracterized its rules.

This is a developing story. Stay tuned to RISMedia for updates.

Jesse Williams contributed to this reporting.

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5520. Spain’s Housing Crisis Sparks a Revolt Against Tourism. Could America Feel the Fallout?

Millions of workers walked off the job across Spain on Wednesday, demanding relief from soaring rents, evictions, and housing speculation. It was the the country's first general strike in 14 years.

In Barcelona, protesters rattled house keys and chanted, “O baixen els lloguers, o cremen els carrers," which translates to “Either rents fall, or the streets burn.”

Over the past decade, rents in the City of Counts have climbed more than 50%, with tourism adding pressure on an already strained housing market.

In the coastal city of Málaga, Mónica Reino, 56, has watched that transformation unfold in her own apartment building.

“Every year it gets worse,” she told AFP, estimating that half of its 20 apartments are now tourist accommodations.

Tourism is far from the only force driving Spain's housing crisis. In popular vacation destinations, property owners can earn more from short-term visitors than year-round tenants, creating a financial incentive to convert residential housing into tourist accommodations.

A day after the strike, lawmakers narrowly approved a package of housing measures, including a new 10% tax on qualifying vacation rentals.

The conflict mirrors one already playing out in vacation destinations across the United States, where booming tourism has helped sustain local economies while putting housing increasingly out of reach for residents.

But as restrictions on vacation rentals make accommodations scarcer and more expensive abroad, could more travelers turn to U.S. destinations, intensifying the housing pressures those communities are already struggling to contain?

Spain's efforts to restrict short-term rentals were already changing the market well before this week's protests and housing vote.

Available short-term rental listings fell 5.9% in October compared with a year earlier, while average nightly rates jumped 12.5%, according to a new analysis from AirDNA, which tracks vacation rentals across platforms such as Airbnb and Vrbo.

Part of the price increase reflects a shift toward more expensive properties as licensing restrictions remove rentals from the market. But even rates for comparable existing properties rose 8.2% over the past year.

Spain had an estimated 355,000 tourist dwellings in 2025, according to the Bank of Spain. Although they represented just 1.5% of the country's housing stock, they accounted for roughly 10% of its rental market, with much higher concentrations in tourist neighborhoods.

Research suggests those concentrations can have substantial consequences for local rents.

Airbnb's expansion pushed residential rents up 7% in Barcelona neighborhoods with the highest levels of activity between 2012 and 2016, according to a 2020 study published in the Journal of Urban Economics. Across the city, the estimated increase was 1.9%.

"Short-term rental activity can crowd locals out of homes that might otherwise serve as conventional rental homes, reducing the number of options available for those living in the area permanently and raising prices," Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com®, says.

But he cautions: "This effect is probably not the main factor affecting affordability."

Even so, Barcelona plans to let all 10,101 existing tourist-apartment licenses expire in 2028, while Málaga has suspended new licenses for three years.

The restrictions could return some tourist accommodations to residential use. Whether enough properties will become available to ease housing costs remains uncertain.

Spain welcomed more than 80.5 million international tourists during the first nine months of 2026—a 5.2% increase over the same period last year. Americans accounted for nearly 3.9 million of those visitors, with arrivals growing more than twice as fast as overall international tourism.

On its face, it's a counterintuitive trend: Higher accommodation costs have hardly deterred American travelers. But part of the explanation may lie in who can afford to keep traveling.

Higher-income households, supported by record household wealth, are driving a disproportionate share of U.S. travel spending, according to the U.S. Travel Association. While rising costs are forcing some households to adjust their plans, wealthier travelers are better positioned to absorb higher prices.

And generational wealth could add to the advantage, too. Visa estimates that $36 trillion will pass from baby boomers to younger generations over the next two decades, with housing and travel among the sectors expected to benefit.

If that pattern sounds familiar, it's because inherited wealth is also helping determine who can afford to own a home at all. In Spain, parents gifted their children more than 30,000 homes last year, while in the U.S., a record 10% of first-time homebuyers relied on an inheritance for their down payment, according to a November report from the National Association of Realtors®.

And if rising accommodation costs abroad encourage more travelers to vacation closer to home, those pressures could intensify.

There's no evidence yet that the restrictions sweeping across Europe are redirecting tourists to U.S. destinations, but domestic demand is already growing fastest in smaller, relatively affordable markets.

Nights booked in small-city and rural U.S. markets increased 8.4% in October from a year earlier, compared with just 1.1% growth in urban markets, according to AirDNA.

"The closest parallels are American tourism hubs where housing is limited and the conversion of homes into STRs force tourism industry workers to live far away," says Berner. "Think Hawaii, Mountain West ski towns, or New Orleans.

"In the more urban locations (like New Orleans), the upward pressure on rent is more concentrated in tourist-heavy neighborhoods than in the metro area at large. But in the more remote destinations without suburbia to absorb displaced locals, the effect is stronger," Berner says.

Nantucket, MA, offers a particularly telling example. The tiny island of just 48 square miles hosts nearly 2 million visitors annually.

More than half of the housing stock (55%) is reserved for seasonal or occasional use, according to a Realtor.com analysis. That scarcity set against high demand has helped push the median home listing price to $4,925,000 in June—more than 11 times the national median of $430,000.

And it's not just lower-income workers being priced out, either.

Roughly 1,080 renter households, including those earning well above the local median income, were effectively shut out of homeownership without significant financial assistance, according to a 2025 housing assessment.

The shortage is so severe that it’s threatening the island's ability to sustain its workforce. A 2026 workforce housing study found that 64% of surveyed employers had lost or declined to hire workers because of housing challenges.

Nantucket Cottage Hospital has identified housing as the leading reason candidates turn down jobs or employees leave.

"Workers get displaced, but communities get hollowed out, too," Berner says. "Schools get weaker, tax bases become more fragile as they are more exposed to tourism downturns, and entry into the community through homeownership becomes more difficult."

For communities that depend on tourism, restricting vacation rentals presents another dilemma: How much visitor spending can they afford to lose in the effort to preserve housing?

On Long Island's North Fork, officials are considering restrictions that would cap short-term rental permits in Southold Town at just 119 properties, compared with approximately 640 active listings in October.

Those rentals generate an estimated $27.5 million in annual revenue for property owners, according to town figures reported by Newsday.

But reducing that business doesn't guarantee more housing for residents. Nearly 37% of the town's housing units were seasonal residences in 2020, and many owners purchased their properties primarily as second homes.

As Realtor.com previously reported, those owners may simply stop offering short-term stays rather than sell their properties or convert them into annual rentals.

Diane Mollica, a local real estate agent with the Gambino Group, says many owners primarily use their properties for their own enjoyment, making a widespread shift to year-round housing unlikely.

Yet the housing shortage is already threatening the businesses that depend on tourism.

"We cannot build a sustainable tourism economy on the backs of a workforce that can no longer afford to live here," Amanda Giuliano, a Southold business owner and co-chair of the town's Economic Development Committee, told Newsday. "If we don't have people working, there will be no tourism."

Spain faces the same conflict on a much larger scale.

Tourism contributed €200.7 billion (about $221 billion) to the Spanish economy in 2024, accounting for 12.6% of GDP, according to the country's National Statistics Institute. The industry supported more than 2.7 million jobs, representing 12.3% of employment nationwide.

That economic dependence helps explain why then, even against a backdrop of a nationwide general strike, the 10% tax on vacation rentals passed only in a 35 to 34 vote.

The new levy is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 1. But even so, the measure could be short-lived. Spain faces a snap election on Nov. 29, triggered by parliament's earlier rejection of the government's housing decrees, and the opposition Popular Party has pledged to repeal the measures if it takes power.

And even if the restrictions survive, reducing tourist accommodations could still come at a cost to the businesses and property owners who depend on them, without producing enough homes for local workers.

Berner argues that increasing housing supply offers a way to accommodate both.

"Encouraging more homebuilding is the only long-term solution to a housing shortage and has the ability to expand tourism capacity as well," he says.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5519. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5518. Thanksgiving Is the Worst Day of the Year for Cooking Fires—Is Your Kitchen Prepared?

If you’re hosting loved ones this Thanksgiving, now is the time to get your kitchen ready. Otherwise, a nice holiday meal could turn into a costly and dangerous ordeal.

According to the latest data from the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), about 1,139 home cooking fires were reported to U.S. fire departments on Thanksgiving Day 2024.

That’s a 321% increase over the daily average, making Turkey Day the leading day of the year for home cooking fires.

“People don’t ever set out to leave the kitchen unattended, but a minute is all it takes for a grease and oil fire to take over, and there’s a greater risk of that happening on Thanksgiving when every burner is going,” says Payton Kashani, personal injury attorney, president, and managing partner of Sunset West Legal Group PC in Los Angeles.

By preparing your kitchen ahead of time, you can reduce the risk of fires and enjoy a delicious and safe celebration with family.

The NFPA says that unattended cooking is the leading cause of home cooking fires. And that’s quite common on Thanksgiving Day.

Many dishes are usually being cooked at once on the stove, oven, and various countertop appliances. Add in a house full of guests that bring constant interruptions and you’re left with a risky situation.

“Thanksgiving fires aren’t usually about cooking appliances going wrong. They tend to happen in those few minutes when someone steps away to greet a guest at the door. Distractions like this can wind up causing serious burns with long, painful recoveries that shake up a family’s normal life,” explains Amanda Demanda, founder of Amanda Demanda Injury Lawyers in Miami.

Grease and oil fires are particularly concerning because there are so many dishes cooking at the same time.

Additionally, despite the fact that the NFPA strongly discourages the use of oil-based turkey fryers due to fire and burn risk, many people put a frozen or wet turkey into hot oil and cause a fire.

“Fires can also stem from flammable items that get left near the stove, like kitchen towels or food packaging. Loose sleeves may get caught up in the mix, and when things catch on fire, many of the injuries that arise happen from people trying to fight the fire themselves,” adds Demanda.

Before Thanksgiving cooking gets underway, prepare your kitchen and anyone who’s going to be in it or near it.

When you’re frying, boiling, or broiling, stay in the kitchen and set timers so you’ll know when dishes are ready. Once they’re done, check that all burners and your oven are off before you leave the room.

Keep everything that can catch fire well away from the burners, oven, or any other appliance that generates heat. These include towels, paper and plastic bags, oven mitts, wooden utensils, and food wrappers.

“If you’re going to wear long sleeves, make sure they’re close-fitting rather than loose,” says Demanda.

Demanda recommends keeping a lid on standby.

Your fire extinguisher should be within reach as well. Just make sure it’s always near the stove and everyone in your home knows how to use it.

In addition, skip the task of oil-frying your turkey if possible. If you like the taste, buy it already fried or use an oil-less fryer instead.

“In the event you do use a traditional fryer, keep it away from your house, place it on a flat, even surface, and ensure [the turkey] is fully thawed,” says Stephanie Fox, national spokesperson at American Red Cross.

Lastly, direct kids and pets out of the cooking area.

“Kids and pets running around your kitchen are a burn injury waiting to happen, so make sure you have a spot for guests to gather away from your cooking zone,” adds Demanda.

Rich Repich, home services expert at Cinch Home Services in Boca Raton, FL, recommends setting up appetizers and drinks in a different room so guests don't crowd the cook and giving them a separate table to leave any used dishes.

#5517. Leaving VMware starts as a cost decision, but day-two operations decide whether it works

Enterprises leaving legacy hypervisors are finding that moving virtual machines is only half the job, and that a portable data management layer often decides whether a Kubernetes migration succeeds. Rising license costs are pushing teams to run containers and VMs on one platform.

That shift is playing out at Mouser Electronics Inc., one of the world’s largest electronic components distributors. After running Red Hat Inc.’s OpenShift for containers for five to six years, the company is now building a production OpenShift Virtualization cluster to move workloads off Broadcom Inc.’s VMware, according to Ronald Waller (pictured, left), systems engineer at Mouser.

“It doesn’t matter if we’re running containers or VMs, we’re running it on the same foundation, which really works well,” Waller said. “Because we can manage those things with the same tool sets and same skill sets.”

Waller and Jon Owings (right), assistant vice president of global technical presales, cloud and data services, at Portworx by Everpure, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the data management layer helps run VMs and containers on OpenShift. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes already serves as a common control plane for containerized AI workloads, and pulling VMs onto it extends that standard to older applications. Everpure Inc., which rebranded from Pure Storage Inc. this year as part of a data-centric pivot, positions Portworx as the matching abstraction for storage.

“Kubernetes provides that ubiquitous control plane for all of them, and that’s what customers are asking us for,” Owings said. “The one thing that was missing was the same thing but for data.”

The learning curve for VMware administrators moving to Kubernetes is steep, and Waller has climbed it over the last year. Storage turned out to be the easy part when he built Mouser’s proof-of-concept cluster, he explained.

“I asked the storage guy what I needed from him, and he handed me a user ID and an API key. I went to Portworx Central. I configured my spec for the operator and the storage cluster, created my secret, and boom, Portworx Enterprise did everything else on the backend,” Waller said. “I didn’t even have to think about it.”

Portworx keeps building for that use case. It made data management native to OpenShift in May and unveiled new AI and VM capabilities at KubeCon. For teams following Mouser’s path, Owings sees the exit from a legacy hypervisor as a chance to rethink day-two operations on a data management layer that travels across clouds and Kubernetes distributions.

“What can we change that we didn’t like about the last 15 years? … Were we dependent on a vendor? Were we dependent on shell scripts or PowerShell?” Owings said. “We have this great opportunity to do something new, and Kubernetes has that open API that allows you to be creative.”

#5516. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5515. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5514. Homeowner’s Massive 60,000-Light Christmas Display Dubbed a Safety Hazard by HOA

'Tis almost the season for goodwill toward all—unless you’re Neil Heuer and his neighbors.

Heuer, a semi-retired tech entrepreneur, lives in Aero Plantation, an exclusive fly-in community in Waxhaw, NC, with his wife and their children. Over the past several months, he’s been locked in a battle with Aero Plantation's HOA over his annual Halloween and Christmas displays, which his neighbors say disrupt the neighborhood and make them feel unsafe.

Heuer has been putting on the light shows, which include more than 60,000 lights, choreographed animatronic displays, and coordinated music programming, for the past five years. He estimates he's spent more than $70,000 on the exhibitions.

But after last year’s shows, his neighbors began complaining. Those complaints led to a hearing, a lawsuit, and proposed potential changes to the HOA’s bylaws that would prohibit Heuer’s Christmas and Halloween spectaculars in the future.

For his part, Heuer believes the drama has little to do with the lights and more to do with a golf course dispute and a once-anonymous newsletter he penned to bring HOA issues to light.

"I realize that this is a little unorthodox, but, you know, everybody celebrates things differently," Heuer says of his light display. "I have friends that celebrate their birthday for the entire month and I might be lucky to have a slice of cake on my birthday, but it doesn't matter. This is this is my hobby. I love to share it with people. I sit outside and record it myself, and I smile. I'm I'm just so giddy with it.""It's it makes me happy, which is good," he continues. "Especially right now because I do feel like it's draining. It's been a very draining experience."

Neil and Stephanie Heuer moved to Aero Plantation, an exclusive fly-in neighborhood that includes a private airstrip, tennis courts, an equestrian center, and other luxury amenities, six years ago.

The Heuer's five-bedroom, 8,000 sq. ft. home sits on 2.36 acres and includes a pool and a four-car garage. Property listing photos show a home hidden in a copse of woods on the edge of a pond.

Heuer told Realtor.com he initially got into the holiday displays because of his interest in tech and because his children enjoyed the shows.

“The kids got a kick out of it, and I thought it was cute,” he says.

His neighbors enjoyed the shows, too, he says.“There's a time I can tell you that our neighbors came over and danced in our driveway. We sat and just talked and sat on the front porch and just... It was really nice," he adds.

Two years ago, though, things took a turn.

Heuer alleges the inciting incident was a disagreement with the HOA board’s vice president over a proposal to “rejuvenate” the community’s golf course. Heuer objected to using reserve funds on the golf course. The vice president offered to pay for the upgrades personally, promising that annual maintenance on the course would be around $8,000, Heuer said.

“After that, I started an anonymous newsletter,” says Heuer, meant to “ask questions”

The newsletter "was critical of the HOA, but there was nobody asking these questions. I was anonymous because I really didn't want to receive backlash for asking questions. I didn't want to be on the receiving side of what I'm experiencing now, basically, if that makes sense.”

When it was uncovered that Heuer was behind the HOA-critical newsletter, “they basically weaponized the HOA against me,” Heuer says.

At this year’s annual community meeting, when it was revealed that the golf course’s upkeep would run closer to $16,000, he brought up the discrepancy.

“Everybody looked around at me and said, ‘Sit down and shut up,” he says.

Heuer contends that those factors—not the light show itself—have upset his neighbors and led to a hearing earlier this year over alleged HOA violations.

In a letter sent to Heuer this past August, the HOA’s legal counsel, Benjamin Karb, wrote that “Inviting unknown members of the public into the subdivision is the type of offensive activity that is a nuisance or annoyance to the neighborhood” and accused Heuer of violating the HOA’s Declaration.

"They believe the roads are private and that nobody belongs here who doesn't live here, I guess," Heuer says. "Let me tell you, 90% of the cars that go by my home I don't recognize. There are people driving by every day who aren't neighbors. And somehow, when they're here to watch my show, they suddenly have a problem. And the people watching my show are families with kids in the backseat."

In September 2026, the HOA held a hearing on the holiday display, alleging it violated the community’s declarations on exterior lighting, signage size, traffic and guest limits, and architectural alterations.

Of major concern was the flow of traffic through the neighborhood by locals looking to see the light show. Aero Plantation is not gated, but it is a private residential community, and the HOA owns and maintains the roads.

In a September 15 letter following the hearing, Karb wrote that when it came to the visitors, the board "did not find a violation exists at this time.”

However, Heuer was found in violation on lighting and signage sizes. The board was unable to make a determination on parking and whether the Heuers had architecturally altered their home’s exterior.

Ironically, the sign that violated the community’s signage limits was one Heuer erected to let visitors know that the off-duty sheriff’s deputies patrolling the neighborhood had been hired by the HOA, not him.

In early October, Heuer filed a lawsuit in North Carolina’s Union Superior Court alleging the HOA overstepped its authority, failed to provide proper notice and hearing procedures, and that the restrictions being enforced had never been formally adopted in the bylaws.

That case is ongoing, but in the meantime, the HOA board sent out a notice that it was adopting new parking rules in the community.

"While normal visits from family, friends, and personal guests are always welcome, the Rules explicitly address situations where activities conducted, sponsored, or permitted by an Owner attract non-resident traffic—even if the Owner did not personally invite or know each visitor. Owners are held directly responsible for any traffic, stopping, or parking resulting from these activities on our private roads," the notice reads.

Around the same time, a notice was sent to homeowners about two proposed amendments to the bylaws, one of which would establish “standards for public attractions and activities that generate substantial or recurring nonresident traffic within the community,” and another that would create “standards for flashing, strobing, pulsating, and high-intensity exterior lighting and authorize the Board to adopt implementing rules consistent with the Declaration.”

The vote on amending the bylaws is scheduled for the end of January, so Heuer plans on going big once more with his holiday display this year.

"Whatever these cockamamie rules that they're trying to change will not apply to this year,” says Heuer.

Realtor.com reached out to the HOA board to inquire about the dispute. In an emailed response, Aero Plantation HOA President David Arno wrote: “Mr. Heuer filed a lawsuit against the Association, to which the Association will respond through the appropriate legal process. The North Carolina Planned Community Act authorizes an HOA’s members to implement additional changes to a Declaration, which is what members are being asked to decide. The Board does not intend to comment further other than to remind members to voice their opinions by deciding if they want to approve the proposed changes or not.”

After a notice about the proposed amendments were sent out, Heuer emailed his neighbors, imploring them to think twice about adding more amendments to the bylaws.

“Look, you may not like our light show, you may like it. But I don't think we need more rules,” he says.

Regardless of the vote's outcome, Heuer and his wife have decided they’re moving out of Aero Plantation as soon as their youngest daughter, currently a sophomore, graduates from high school.

"There's two things I can assure you," he says. "One is that I will not live here after my daughter graduates. And my next neighborhood will not have an HOA."

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5513. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5512. Savannah Guthrie Extends NBC News Contract as Search Continues for Her Mother, Nancy Guthrie

To see our latest updates on the Nancy Guthrie case, please click here.

Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, solidifying her spot as a co-anchor on “Today.”

The decision comes months after it was previously reported that the host was expected to “never return” to her on-air role, as she waited for answers regarding the Feb. 1 kidnapping of her mother, Nancy Guthrie.

Guthrie, 54, returned to the show—and her home in New York City—after a six-week hiatus.

“Savannah is the best in the business,” a Page Six source said on Nov. 12. “We want her to stay for as long as she wants to stay.”

In 2024, the outlet previously reported that the journalist—who joined “Today” in June 2011 as chief legal correspondent and a co-host of the show’s third hour—earns between $7 and $8 million annually.

A People magazine source described Guthrie as “not only so unbelievably strong,” but as “the glue that keeps the show together.”

Authorities are still investigating her 84-year-old mother’s abduction from her Tucson, AZ home—and Guthrie continues to feel the weight of the tragedy each day.

“It’s always with me,” she shared during a June episode of the morning news show. “I cry every morning on the way to work, and I cry every morning on the way home.”

The most recent update in the case comes with a former FBI agent’s revelation that she had received four disturbing ransom messages concerning Nancy’s disappearance. The former agent, Jennifer Coffindaffer, shared she had been targeted by individuals claiming to have information about the disappearance, and demanding cryptocurrency in exchange for her return.

Coffindaffer could not confirm the authenticity of the communications, and believed the messages may have been sent by individuals hoping to capitalize on the high-profile investigation.

The former agent passed the communications to the FBI. The bureau was able to confirm that the cryptocurrency wallet address provided did not correspond with those associated with previous ransom notes investigators considered to be potentially authentic.

Anyone with any information about Nancy Guthrie's case should call 1-800-CALL-FBI, 520-351-4900, or 88-CRIME, or visit tips.fbi.gov.

Coffindaffer had initially chosen not to share the emails publicly, but had a change of heart after Lauren Serpa, a woman who lives near Nancy’s home, had received and shared similar communications—which included unsettling photos of Nancy and religious references that appeared to be tailored to the family’s Catholic faith.

Coffindaffer had become concerned that others following the investigation could become targets for individuals seeking money.

Guthrie has made a series of public pleas, in hopes of sharing a “very specific message” with the individuals who could have information about her mother’s disappearance.

“It has been months since our mom was taken from us. Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part. But we will never stop looking for her,” she said in a July statement shared to Instagram.

“We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts,” she continued. “The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place, and I know that you have tried to do things the right way, so I am asking you, begging you to do the right thing now.”

Guthrie closed the statement with an ask for help, and a promise that it’s “never too late to do the right thing.”

“I always believe there is a way home,” she said. “Please make the right choice.”

Nancy was first reported missing at around 12 p.m. local time on Feb. 1, around 14 hours after she was dropped off at the property following a family dinner. When she failed to turn up at her usual church gathering on Sunday, her friends alerted her family, who found her home was empty.

Officials have noted during a Feb. 5 media briefing that, while times are approximate, the team pieced together several pieces of evidence to indicate Nancy's movements—and the timeline of her apparent abduction.

5:32 p.m. Nancy travels to Annie's house in an Uber for "dinner and playing games with the family."

9:48 p.m. A garage door at Nancy's house opens when she was dropped off at the property by her daughter.

9:50 p.m. The garage door closes, indicating that Nancy was inside the home.

1:47 a.m. Nancy's doorbell security camera is disconnected.

2:12 a.m. Movement is detected on a security camera at the home. No footage of this is currently available.

2:28 a.m. Nancy's pacemaker app indicates that the device has been disconnected from her phone.

11:00 a.m. Nancy fails to arrive at the home of a friend, where she had been due to watch a church service livestream.

11:56 a.m. Nancy's family travels to her home to check on her and finds the property empty.

12:03 p.m. The family calls 911 to report Nancy missing.

12:14 p.m. Police officers arrive at Nancy's home.

Police uncovered evidence inside the property suggesting the 84-year-old was "taken" from her home against her will, and "harmed" during the alleged "abduction."

Law enforcement still had no suspects, but were investigating multiple ransom notes and tips providing potentially helpful information.

Savannah Guthrie releases her first public plea, asking for help in finding her missing mother.

Authorities detained a man for questioning after reviewing footage of a masked, armed intruder tampering with a security camera outside of Nancy's home. It was unclear if the person who was questioned was the same individual from the footage.

The FBI announced it was conducting a new "extensive" search for Nancy in the area surrounding her Arizona home. The Pima County Sheriff's Department noted it had received nearly 18,000 calls about the case, and that "several hundred detectives and agents" were assigned to the ongoing investigation.

The Guthrie family was officially cleared as suspects.

Law enforcement officials revealed the kidnapper had a "target."

"I think this was an individual who had a target for whatever reason, and he has made it tough, but I've got some pretty tough investigators, too," Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos shared.

Guthrie broke down in tears as she offered a reward of up to $1 million for anyone who was able to provide information leading to the recovery of her mother.

It was reported that the FBI decided to pull nearly all of the agents assigned to the case out of Tucson and return them to the agency's Phoenix headquarters.

A man was arrested outside of Nancy's home on DUI charges after he was seen driving past the property "50 to 100 times" while looking at a photo of the missing woman on his phone. A spokesperson confirmed the arrest, but noted it had no connection to Nancy's case.

Additional evidence was identified—ranging from DNA found on various objects and thumbnail images from motion-activated cameras in Nancy's backyard—but the search continues.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.
