#5482. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5481. Microsoft 365 Outage: CIOs Should Verify Recovery Across Workflows and Security Controls, Says Infotech

The Microsoft 365 outage has shown how email dependencies can interrupt business processes even when other functions remain available. Infotech's research note, Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs, covers recovery validation, potential security coverage gaps, and continuity measures for prolonged cloud outages.

ARLINGTON, Va., Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- In response to the Microsoft 365 outage that began on November 12, Infotech, a global research and API-driven advisory firm, is recommending that CIOs verify the recovery of business-critical workflows, integrations, and security controls before declaring normal operations restored. The firm's new research note, Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs, also advises organizations to document service disruptions and preserve evidence for potential service level agreement claims.

The outage began Thursday afternoon with Exchange Online mailbox access failures in the Americas and affected functions in Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender. Thursday night, servers that had returned to service failed again under load, and Microsoft added capacity and began rolling back a recent network change. According to the note's midday ET update on November 13, availability was improving, but intermittent issues persisted, and Microsoft had not given a restoration time. At that point, Microsoft had reported no evidence of malicious activity, and the root cause was still under investigation.

"CIOs need a clear basis for telling the business it can return to normal operations," says Kate Wood, AVP of Research Development at Infotech. "That means knowing which critical processes have been tested, where security coverage still needs checking, and which teams must continue using workarounds. Executive updates should make those outstanding issues visible so that business teams can plan their next steps."

The examples summarized in Infotech's note show contingency plans holding where a manual route existed and stalling where email was the only channel. According to news reports, disruptions included delays to patient referrals and court communications, while some organizations maintained critical operations using other systems or manual procedures. Core Teams messaging and meetings and direct SharePoint file access also remained largely operational, reinforcing the need to assess the specific functions and dependencies supporting each business process.

Recommended Actions for Microsoft 365 Response and RecoveryInfotech advises CIOs to focus on maintaining operations and documenting impacts. IT teams should log unresolved issues and failed workarounds throughout recovery, giving executives a clear view of operating status and creating a record to guide improvements to continuity plans.

The firm's Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs research note groups its recommendations as follows:

For longer-term readiness, Infotech emphasizes testing continuity procedures against prolonged outages affecting multiple cloud services. Organizations should identify where reliance on a single cloud environment creates shared points of failure and establish independent continuity options where the business impact justifies them.

Additional resources include the firm's Develop a Business Continuity Plan, Create a Right-Sized Disaster Recovery Plan, and IT Communications Research Center.

#5480. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5479. IRS raises 401(k) limit for 2027 to $25,500

The IRS increased the 2027 401(k) deferral limit to $25,500 and raised catch-up limits to $8,500, or $11,750 for ages 60 to 63. IRA limits remain at $7,500, while multiple IRA and Saver’s Credit income thresholds increased.  AI Summary

The IRS has increased the annual contribution limit for 401(k) plans in 2027 to $25,500, up $1,000 from the 2026 limit of $24,500, the agency announced on Thursday.

The higher limit also applies to employees participating in 403(b) plans, governmental 457 plans and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan, according to guidance issued by the IRS in Notice 2026-66. The notice outlines cost-of-living adjustments for retirement plans and other retirement-related tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

The catch-up contribution limit for employees ages 50 and older increased to $8,500, up from $8,000 in 2026. That brings the total annual contribution limit for most eligible participants ages 50 and older to $34,000.

Employees ages 60 through 63 are eligible for a higher catch-up contribution limit under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022. For 2027, that limit increased to $11,750, allowing eligible participants to contribute up to $37,250.

The annual contribution limit for individual retirement accounts remains unchanged at $7,500. The IRA catch-up contribution limit for individuals ages 50 and older also remains at $1,100.

“Along with the Working Families Tax Cuts, this increase in the pension limitations will help American families keep more of their hard-earned income,” IRS CEO Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.

The IRS also increased several income thresholds used to determine eligibility for tax deductions and retirement account contributions.

For traditional IRAs, the income phase-out range for single taxpayers covered by a workplace retirement plan increased to $83,000 to $93,000, up from $81,000 to $91,000 in 2026.

For married couples filing jointly, the range increased to $133,000 to $153,000, up from $129,000 to $149,000, when the spouse making the contribution is covered by a workplace retirement plan.

For IRA contributors who are not covered by a workplace retirement plan but are married to someone who is, the phase-out range increased to $250,000 to $260,000, up from $242,000 to $252,000.

The income phase-out range for Roth IRA contributions also increased. For single taxpayers and heads of household, the range is now $158,000 to $173,000, compared with $153,000 to $168,000 in 2026. For married couples filing jointly, it increased to $250,000 to $260,000, up from $242,000 to $252,000.

The IRS also raised the annual contribution limit for SIMPLE retirement accounts to $17,500, up from $17,000. Certain eligible SIMPLE plans have a higher limit of $19,100, compared with $18,100 in 2026.

Catch-up contribution limits for most SIMPLE plans remain unchanged at $4,000 for employees ages 50 and older. The limit is $3,850 for certain applicable SIMPLE plans and $5,250 for employees ages 60 through 63.

The income limits for the Saver’s Credit, which benefits low- and moderate-income workers who save for retirement, also increased. For 2027, the limits are $83,000 for married couples filing jointly, $62,250 for heads of household, and $41,500 for single taxpayers and married individuals filing separately.

The IRS said the adjustments are intended to account for cost-of-living changes and help taxpayers and employers plan for the coming year.

#5478. Microsoft 365 Outage: CIOs Should Verify Recovery Across Workflows and Security Controls, Says Infotech

The Microsoft 365 outage has shown how email dependencies can interrupt business processes even when other functions remain available. Infotech's research note, Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs, covers recovery validation, potential security coverage gaps, and continuity measures for prolonged cloud outages.

ARLINGTON, Va., Nov. 13, 2026 /CNW/ -- In response to the Microsoft 365 outage that began on November 12, Infotech, a global research and API-driven advisory firm, is recommending that CIOs verify the recovery of business-critical workflows, integrations, and security controls before declaring normal operations restored. The firm's new research note, Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs, also advises organizations to document service disruptions and preserve evidence for potential service level agreement claims.

The outage began Thursday afternoon with Exchange Online mailbox access failures in the Americas and affected functions in Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender. Thursday night, servers that had returned to service failed again under load, and Microsoft added capacity and began rolling back a recent network change. According to the note's midday ET update on November 13, availability was improving, but intermittent issues persisted, and Microsoft had not given a restoration time. At that point, Microsoft had reported no evidence of malicious activity, and the root cause was still under investigation.

"CIOs need a clear basis for telling the business it can return to normal operations," says Kate Wood, AVP of Research Development at Infotech. "That means knowing which critical processes have been tested, where security coverage still needs checking, and which teams must continue using workarounds. Executive updates should make those outstanding issues visible so that business teams can plan their next steps."

The examples summarized in Infotech's note show contingency plans holding where a manual route existed and stalling where email was the only channel. According to news reports, disruptions included delays to patient referrals and court communications, while some organizations maintained critical operations using other systems or manual procedures. Core Teams messaging and meetings and direct SharePoint file access also remained largely operational, reinforcing the need to assess the specific functions and dependencies supporting each business process.

Recommended Actions for Microsoft 365 Response and RecoveryInfotech advises CIOs to focus on maintaining operations and documenting impacts. IT teams should log unresolved issues and failed workarounds throughout recovery, giving executives a clear view of operating status and creating a record to guide improvements to continuity plans.

The firm's Microsoft 365 Outage: Immediate Actions for CIOs research note groups its recommendations as follows:

For longer-term readiness, Infotech emphasizes testing continuity procedures against prolonged outages affecting multiple cloud services. Organizations should identify where reliance on a single cloud environment creates shared points of failure and establish independent continuity options where the business impact justifies them.

Additional resources include the firm's Develop a Business Continuity Plan, Create a Right-Sized Disaster Recovery Plan, and IT Communications Research Center.

#5477. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5476. Mortgage industry expects CFPB servicing rule to narrow

The CFPB has sent a revised version of its 2024 “Streamlining Mortgage Servicing for Borrowers Experiencing Payment Difficulties” rule to the Office of Management and Budget, moving closer to finalizing new loss-mitigation standards under Regulation X. Industry attorneys expect a significantly narrower rule than the original proposal, shaped by President Trump’s directive to modernize Dodd-Frank-era rules and broad stakeholder pushback against open-ended requirements.  AI Summary

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) last week took another step toward finalizing new loss-mitigation standards, sending a revised version of its 2024 mortgage servicing proposal to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review.

The final rule, “Streamlining Mortgage Servicing for Borrowers Experiencing Payment Difficulties” under Regulation X, is expected to be narrower than the 2024 proposal advanced when the CFPB was led by Rohit Chopra, according to industry attorneys. The CFPB did not immediately reply to HousingWire‘s request for comments.

The move comes in the wake of President Donald Trump’s March 13 executive order, “Promoting Access to Mortgage Credit,” which directs the CFPB to modernize Dodd-Frank-era rules that lenders and servicers say increase compliance costs. The current standards were finalized in 2013.

“We won’t know the final rule’s content until it is published. But the comment record and the current Bureau’s priorities point toward a significantly narrower rule,”Joseph M. DeFazio and Joe Reilly, partners at Troutman Pepper Locke, wrote in a blog post. “Since President Trump’s second term began, the Bureau has also rescinded prior guidance and signaled that it prefers clear, fixed rules to open-ended frameworks like the one in the 2024 proposal.”

The CFPB received more than 80 comments on the proposal, with what the attorneys described as an “unusual degree of convergence” among groups that rarely agree.

The American Bankers Association (ABA) has urged the CFPB to finalize only a limited portion of the 2024 proposal, pressing the bureau to focus on targeted changes rather than a full rewrite.

“The Bureau’s 2024 proposal was founded on the misconception that servicers prioritize foreclosure over helping borrowers find a successful solution to resolve their payment disruptions,” Teshale Smith, the ABA’s senior counsel for regulatory compliance and policy, said in a letter to the CFPB in June. “In fact, sustained low foreclosure rates and high customer satisfaction rates demonstrate that servicers remain committed to helping struggling borrowers.”

The 2024 proposed rule aimed to make permanent several pandemic-era practices used when large numbers of borrowers needed fast assistance. Industry estimates showed that 8.8 million families were helped, with the re-default rate for loans exiting COVID-19 loss-mitigation programs at about 10%, ABA said in its letter.The proposal allows servicers to evaluate loss-mitigation options before borrowers complete an application, prohibits late fees and other charges while a loss-mitigation review is underway, and makes assistance possible in multiple languages.As it relates to foreclosure, the draft allows a loss-mitigation review cycle to start when the borrower asks for help, not only after a completed application, lasting until the loan is current or all options are ruled out. During that time, servicers could not begin or advance foreclosure, a protection that currently applies only after a complete application is on file. Foreclosure could resume only after options were exhausted or the borrower stopped communicating.

Attorneys at Troutman Pepper Locke expect the final rule to permit sequential review of loss-mitigation options instead of requiring servicers to evaluate all options at once; dropping the proposed ban on fee accrual during loss-mitigation reviews; and removal of the language access provisions that were part of the 2024 draft.

Isaac Boltansky, head of public policy at Pennymac, said the company “supports clear, consistent standards that give servicers the certainty they need to deliver the best possible outcomes for homeowners, particularly those facing financial hardship.”

#5475. Mirendil raises $1B in funding to speed up AI model development

Mirendil Inc., a provider of software that speeds up artificial intelligence development, has raised $1 billion in early-stage funding.

The startup stated on Thursday that Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital jointly led the Series A investment. They were joined by more than a half-dozen others including Google LLC.

Mirendil was launched last year by two former Google DeepMind and Anthropic PBC researchers. Chief Executive Officer Behnam Neyshabur is a co-inventor of SAM, a popular algorithm that makes AI models better at tasks they were not specifically trained to perform. Chief Technology Officer Harsh Mehta, in turn, spent his time at Google DeepMind and Anthropic working on pretraining projects. Pretraining is a term for the initial phase of the AI development workflow.

Mirendil’s first product, Lor, is a platform that automates many of the tasks involved in model training runs. The company says that the software does so by splitting work among hundreds of AI agents.

Large language model development involves a significant amount of trial and error. Researchers create multiple versions of an algorithm that differ from one another in small ways and compare them to find the most performant variant. According to Mirendil, Lor can automate that workflow. If an error crops up during the evaluation, the platform fixes it automatically.

Earlier this year, Mirendil asked one of its researchers to build a coding model that can compete with leading open-source LLMs. Usually, such projects are carried out by teams of specialists. Mirendil says that its automation technology enabled the researcher to build the model without any help from colleagues. The project cost $10 million and took about 3.5 months to complete.

The company’s agents wrote more than 99% of the code that powers the model, which is called Mirendil-Base. They set up infrastructure, found a suitable training algorithm and collected training data from the web. The agents then refined both the training dataset and Mirendil-Base’s architecture to boost output quality.

The LLM is the foundation of a specialized coding model called Fern that the company unveiled last month. According to Mirendil, it’s designed to automate programming challenges commonly encountered by AI labs. Fern can process 10 million input tokens per prompt, or 10 times more than Claude Opus 5.5. That’s the equivalent of about a half-million lines of code.

Fern is based on a version of Mirendil-Base with 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Late last month, the company previewed two upgraded versions of the latter model with between 500 billion and 10 trillion parameters. Mirendil plans to use those algorithms to develop more capable LLMs.

#5474. Fly-E Group, Inc. Announces Second Quarter and First Half of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results

NEW YORK, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fly-E Group, Inc. (Nasdaq: FLYE) ("Fly-E" or the "Company"), an electric vehicle company engaged in designing, installing, selling, and renting smart electric motorcycles, electric bikes, and electric scooters, today announced its unaudited financial results for the second quarter and first half of fiscal year 2027 ended September 30, 2026.

Second quarter of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Summary

Mr. Zhou (Andy) Ou, Chief Executive Officer of Fly-E, commented, "During the second quarter, our operational network stabilized following the retail restructuring, with our top-line revenue holding steady sequentially. Our wholesale revenues grew 21.4% year-over-year and accounted for a significantly higher proportion of our total revenue. This evolving revenue mix, combined with promotional pricing in our retail business, naturally influenced our overall margin profile for the period. Meanwhile, we continued to control store-level costs and address corporate matters carefully to strengthen the Company's foundation for the future. By maintaining our operational network and disciplined cost management, we are dedicated to preserving business stability while positioning Fly-E to explore strategic opportunities for long-term growth."

Second quarter of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results

Net revenues were $2.6 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 33.7% from $3.9 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily driven by a lower sales volume of 7,392 units in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to 18,564 in the same period last year, resulting from the reduction in our direct retail store count to four stores as of September 30, 2026, compared to 11 stores as of September 30, 2025.

Cost of revenues was $2.4 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 18.8% from $2.9 million in the same period last year, primarily aligning with lower sales volume driven by the downsizing of our retail store network.

Gross profit was $0.2 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to $1.0 million in the same period last year. Gross margin was 8.1% in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to 25.0% in the same period last year. The decrease in gross margin was primarily attributable to a structural mix shift from direct retail toward lower-priced wholesale channels, further impacted by competitive retail pricing and inventory clearance discounts.

Total operating expenses were $1.8 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 9.8% compared to $2.0 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily attributable to store-level operational savings, which were partially offset by increases in expected credit losses and professional fees.

Net loss was $1.7 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to $1.8 million in the same period last year.

Basic and Diluted Earnings (Losses) per Share

Basic and diluted losses per share were $1.07 in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to $2.18 in the same period last year.

EBITDA was negative $1.3 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, compared to negative EBITDA of $1.0 million in the same period last year.

First Half of Fiscal Year 2027 Financial Results

Net revenues were $5.3 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 42.2% from $9.2 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily driven by a significant reduction in direct retail store counts, resulting in a lower sales volume of 14,950 units in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to 29,012 in the same period last year.

Cost of revenues was $4.8 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 19.5% from $6.0 million in the same period last year, primarily reflecting lower sales volume following the downsizing of our retail store network.

Gross profit was $0.5 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to $3.2 million in the same period last year. Gross margin was 9.5% in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to 35.1% in the same period last year. The decrease in gross margin was primarily attributable to the greater revenue percentage of wholesale channels at lower-priced wholesale pricing, as well as promotional retail pricing adjustment and inventory clearance discounts.

Total operating expenses were $5.7 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, a decrease of 2.2% compared to $5.8 million in the same period last year. The decrease was primarily attributable to operational cost savings from retail store reductions, which were offset by increases in expected credit losses and software development fees.

Net loss was $5.6 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to $3.8 million in the same period last year.

Basic and Diluted Earnings (Losses) per Share

Basic and diluted losses per share were $3.48 in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to $6.58 in the same period last year.

EBITDA was negative $4.7 million in the first half of fiscal year 2027, compared to negative EBITDA of $2.2 million in the same period last year.

As of September 30, 2026, the Company had cash of $0.5 million, compared to $0.3 million as of March 31, 2026.

Fly-E Group, Inc. is an electric vehicle company that is principally engaged in designing, installing, selling, and renting smart electric motorcycles, electric bikes, and electric scooters under the brand "Fly E-Bike." The Company's commitment is to encourage people to incorporate eco-friendly transportation into their active lifestyles, ultimately contributing towards building a more environmentally friendly future. For more information, please visit the Company's website: https://investors.flyebike.com.

To supplement our financial information presented in accordance with the generally accepted accounting principles in the United States (the "U.S. GAAP"), management periodically uses certain "non-GAAP financial measures," as such term is defined under the rules of the SEC, to clarify and enhance understanding of past performance and prospects for the future. Generally, a non-GAAP financial measure is a numerical measure of a company's operating performance, financial position or cash flows that excludes or includes amounts that are included in or excluded from the most directly comparable measure calculated and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP. For example, non-GAAP measures may exclude the impact of certain items such as acquisitions, divestitures, gains, losses and impairments, or items outside of management's control. Management believes that the following non-GAAP financial measure provides investors and analysts useful insight into our financial position and operating performance. Any non-GAAP measure provided should be viewed in addition to, and not as an alternative to, the most directly comparable measure determined in accordance with U.S. GAAP. Further, the calculation of these non-GAAP financial measures may differ from the calculation of similarly titled financial measures presented by other companies and therefore may not be comparable among companies.

We use EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization) to evaluate our operating performance. We believe EBITDA provides additional insight into our underlying, ongoing operating performance and facilitates year-to-year comparisons by excluding the earnings impact of interest, tax, depreciation and amortization and that presenting EBITDA is more representative of our operational performance and may be more useful for investors.

We reconcile our non-GAAP financial measure to our net income, which is our most directly comparable financial measure calculated and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP. EBITDA includes adjustments for provision for income taxes, as applicable, interest income and expense, depreciation, and amortization. EBITDA does not represent and should not be considered an alternative to net income as determined by U.S. GAAP, and our calculations thereof may not be comparable to those reported by other companies. We believe EBITDA is an important measure of operating performance and provides useful information to investors because it highlights trends in our business that may not otherwise be apparent when relying solely on U.S. GAAP measures and because it eliminates items that have less bearing on our operating performance. EBITDA, as presented herein, is a supplemental measure of our performance that is not required by, or presented in accordance with, U.S. GAAP. We use non-GAAP financial measures as supplements to our U.S. GAAP results in order to provide a more complete understanding of the factors and trends affecting our business. EBITDA is a measure of operating performance that is not defined by U.S. GAAP and should not be considered a substitute for net (loss) income as determined in accordance with U.S. GAAP.

#5473. Builder credit conditions tighten for 19th straight quarter

NAHB’s Q3 2026 AD&C Financing survey shows credit for land acquisition, development and construction tightened for the 19th consecutive quarter, mirroring Federal Reserve loan officer data. Contract rates moved only modestly and were offset by lower points, keeping effective borrowing costs elevated across most AD&C categories. Builders are increasingly using construction-to-permanent loans tied to end buyers, with 32% of respondents using them and, for those, 58% of homes financed this way. Persistent tight AD&C lending threatens to slow lot development and new-home supply, reinforcing structural housing shortages even as the mortgage market shows its own signs of stress.  AI Summary

Credit conditions for residential land acquisition, development and construction (AD&C) loans tightened again in the third quarter of 2026, extending a nearly five-year stretch of more restrictive lending for homebuilders, according to a National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) survey.

NAHB’s quarterly AD&C Financing survey showed a net easing index of -15.3 in Q3, meaning more builders and developers reported tighter credit than easier credit. It marks the 19th consecutive quarter of net tightening for AD&C borrowers, NAHB economist Paul Emrath wrote in an analysis published Nov. 13.

The findings closely track the Federal Reserve’s October survey of senior loan officers. NAHB reported that the Fed’s net easing index for residential AD&C loans came in at -15.5 in the third quarter. Aside from modest lender-reported easing in the second quarter of 2026, both lenders and builders have indicated that AD&C credit has been tightening steadily since early 2022. The Fed’s index has been in negative territory in 18 of the past 19 quarters.

For homebuilders and land developers, those readings underscore that bank appetite for risk in residential construction remains weak even as broader housing demand depends on new supply.

While credit availability continued to contract, AD&C financing costs showed only modest quarter-to-quarter movement in the third quarter, with no clear trend toward either higher or lower overall borrowing costs.

NAHB reported the following changes in average contract interest rates between the second and third quarters of 2026:

At the same time, initial points on AD&C loans declined across all four categories, NAHB found:

Those offsetting moves left effective borrowing costs — which combine contract rates and points — little changed for most types of AD&C credit:

For builders, the message is that even where nominal rates tick lower, the all-in cost of capital for lots and vertical construction remains high by historical standards. Combined with tighter underwriting, that environment can slow lot pipeline development, constrain spec building and push more risk and cost back onto builders’ balance sheets.

NAHB’s third-quarter survey also highlighted increased use of construction-to-permanent, or one-time-close, loans tied directly to the end buyer.

Among survey respondents who built single-family homes in the third quarter, 32% said they financed at least some production with construction-to-permanent loans to the ultimate homebuyer. On average, 58% of the homes those respondents built were financed this way, NAHB reported.

Those structures can help builders reduce their direct exposure to AD&C credit by shifting some financing to retail mortgage channels earlier in the process. They can also appeal to buyers looking to lock both construction and permanent financing terms in a single transaction, an important hedge in a volatile rate environment.

NAHB noted that market stress in residential mortgages – including a recent drop in applications and rising delinquencies – has drawn significant attention. But the group argued that constrained AD&C financing is an underappreciated bottleneck for adding new supply, especially in affordable and entry-level segments.

Because AD&C loans finance land pipelines, infrastructure and vertical construction, persistently tight lending standards can limit lot development, delay projects and reduce the number of homes that reach the for-sale market. That dynamic can amplify the impact of low existing-home inventory and keep upward pressure on home prices and rents.

For builders, developers and their lenders, the survey results suggest that planning assumptions for 2027 should continue to factor in restricted credit availability, elevated effective borrowing costs and a need for diversified capital sources, including joint ventures, private capital and greater use of buyer-based construction-to-perm structures.

More detail on credit conditions for residential builders and developers, including cross-tabs on lender behavior and loan terms, is available on NAHB’s AD&C Financing Survey web page.

#5472. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5470. Why Midwest buyer demand is holding up in the face of higher mortgage rates

Midwest metros, including Columbus and Cincinnati, are keeping pending sales near or above new listings as mortgage activity stays mixed. Lower list prices and smaller loan amounts appear to support demand, even with rates above 7% pressuring affordability.  AI Summary

Several Midwest housing markets are showing signs of resilient buyer demand compared to other parts of the country, with pending home sales keeping pace with new listings even as purchase mortgage activity remains largely flat or declines.

Columbus, Ohio, had 127 pending sales for every 100 new listings as of Nov. 6, according to HousingWire Data. Cincinnati followed at 125. These markets were well above the national average of 95 pending sales per 100 new listings, while Cleveland (91) and St. Louis (90) were running slightly below the U.S. average.

The same markets also had median list prices that were considerably lower than the national average of $429,000. Cleveland led the way at $174,000, followed by St. Louis ($225,000), Columbus ($255,000) and Cincinnati ($300,000).

In St. Louis, buyers remain active despite elevated mortgage rates, although they are being more deliberate about their decisions, said Greg Iverson, a divisional sales manager for Neighborhood Loans.

“I wouldn’t say it’s necessarily a buyer’s market, but it’s starting to become that way in certain areas,” Iverson said in an interview with HousingWire.

Like most buyers nationwide, affordability remains the biggest obstacle for his clients, Iverson said. Mortgage rates above 7% have added to the rising costs of property taxes, homeowners insurance, building materials and home repairs. Inventory has also increased in some price ranges, he said, but not across the board.

But Iverson said St. Louis continues to see activity from first-time and move-up buyers alike since the market’s lower home prices have helped keep these buyers from being priced out entirely.

A similar pattern is playing out in smaller Ohio markets. Scott Snapp, a Findlay, Ohio-based branch manager at loanDepot, said his business has remained steady, with loan applications coming in at about the same pace as last year.

When comparing his October 2026 production with the same point a year earlier, Snapp said he had closed 57 loans totaling $12 million last year, versus 51 loans totaling $11 million at the time of the interview. Snapp said his average loan size is about $215,000.

“I’m not seeing a drop, realistically,” he said. “Applications coming in are still at the same pace as they were last year around here.”

Mortgage data platform Modex shows that purchase lending has been relatively steady in several Midwest markets, but it has not uniformly increased.

Cleveland was the only one of four Midwest metros in HousingWire’s comparison to record year-over-year growth in purchase loans from January through July, with 11,809 loans, up 0.9%. Cincinnati recorded 14,048 loans, down 2.2%, while Columbus had 12,820, down 2.7%. St. Louis recorded 9,811 loans, a 6.8% decline. The St. Louis figure excludes St. Louis County since 2026 county records were still being updated.

Modex data indicated that median purchase loan amounts in these Midwest markets ranged from $217,075 in Cleveland to $294,566 in Columbus. Lower loan amounts and home prices could attest to some of the Midwest’s relative resilience. More than 20% of purchase loans in Cleveland and St. Louis were for less than $150,000.

But the resilience is still being tested. Jason Harris, a Columbus-based branch manager at Rate, described September as a slow month for contracts that would have closed in October. And he expected October to be one of the slower months the market had seen in years due to higher mortgage rates.

But he added that contract activity improved over the course of October as mortgage rates eased.

“I feel blessed to be in Columbus because it’s still an area where you can purchase an affordable home,” Harris said. “Affordability is something that is so desperately needed by buyers right now. … Even three-eighths of a percent is having a meaningful impact on demand.”

Harris said first-time buyers, as well as borrowers using down payment assistance and state bond programs, typically make up a larger share of his business late in the year. These buyers, coupled with lower-priced homes, typically bring down his average loan size in the fourth quarter, while also driving more Federal Housing Administration loans and government-backed adjustable-rate mortgages, he said.

Back in St. Louis, Iverson said the metro area has continued to attract interest from real estate investors, including those who are becoming more selective about where they purchase as costs rise in other markets.

Snapp also pointed to local employment as a source of housing demand in his part of Ohio, citing new distribution centers and business activity, including facilities opened by Amazon and planned by Sheetz.

“We’re seeing a lot of businesses coming into this area and opening up, and that’s helped us,” he said.

The market has also benefited from buyers relocating from other states, Snapp said. Some have moved for work, while others are returning to the area to be near family.

St. Louis and smaller Ohio markets contrast with areas where mortgage professionals have reported weaker activity. Iverson said he has heard of homes sitting longer in markets such as San Diego, while Snapp said colleagues in Las Vegas and Seattle had described slower conditions.

Harris said he expects demand in central Ohio to pick up again as the market moves into 2027, even if some buyers are postponing purchases until the spring. He said the region’s underlying need for housing remains strong.

“The number of people that need homes and want homes in central Ohio over the next five years is going to be good,” he said.

#5467. Will the Fifth Circuit keep FinCEN anti-money laundering rule off the books?

ALTA and TLTA urged the Fifth Circuit to uphold a March ruling that vacated FinCEN’s residential real estate AML reporting rule. The groups argue FinCEN underestimated compliance costs and exceeded its authority under the Bank Secrecy Act.  AI Summary

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network’s (FinCEN) Residential Real Estate Rule is not currently in effect and the American Land Title Association (ALTA) and the Texas Land Title Association (TLTA) would like it to stay that way.

In late October, ALTA and TLTA filed amicus briefs asking the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit to uphold a ruling that vacated FinCEN’s nationwide anti-money laundering (AML) rule.

The AML rule mandated reporting for any non-financed residential real estate transfer where ownership was held by an entity or trust — with no geographic or price threshold.

The rule was overturned in late March by a federal judge in the Eastern District of Texas after the law had been in effect for less than three weeks. In early May, FinCEN appealed the ruling.

This ruling and subsequent appeal are part of a lawsuit filed by Flowers Title Companies, LLC, which argued that FinCEN lacked authority under the Bank Secrecy Act to impose such sweeping reporting requirements.

In their briefs ALTA and TLTA argued that the rule “imposes significant costs and operational burdens on title and settlement professionals without adequately demonstrating that its benefits justify those requirements.”

According to ALTA, FinCEN’s cost estimate of implementing the policy of $559.4 million was too low, as the association felt FinCEN did not fully account for the cost to title companies for employee training, technology changes, record keeping and the time it takes to get information from buyers and sellers. Additionally, ALTA argues that title professionals have no authority to force buyers or sellers to provide them with beneficial ownership information and that financial institutions already collect beneficial ownership information from their business customers when accounts are opened.

In its filing, TLTA adds that the transactions FinCEN’s rule targets are routine and legal, noting that FinCEN’s legal authority only applies to “suspicious” transactions, not an entire class of transaction.

It remains to be seen how the appeals court will rule on this issue. However, FinCEN has also said it will not require retroactive reporting for transactions that would have been reportable during these legal proceedings.

FinCEN had argued the rule was necessary to close loopholes that allowed money launderers, drug traffickers and other illicit actors to use shell companies and trusts to purchase property with anonymity.

Fidelity National Financial (FNF) has also challenged FinCEN’s AML rule in court, but this resulted in the rule being upheld. That decision has since been appealed by FNF in the Eleventh Circuit.

#5466. Stubborn input inflation pressures builders despite energy pullback

NAHB’s analysis of the October Producer Price Index shows total inputs to new residential construction up 0.3% on the month and 10.4% year over year, outpacing overall PPI inflation. Goods costs were flat in October, but building materials rose 0.5% and 5.8% annually, with diesel, plywood and board products elevated. Service inputs climbed 0.7% in October and 11.3% year over year, led by double-digit gains in trade services and transportation. The data underscores ongoing pressure on bids, budgets and pro formas, even as headline energy prices ease.  AI Summary

Residential construction input costs continued to outpace overall inflation in October, as gains in building material and service prices offset a monthly decline in energy, according to a National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) analysis of this morning’s Producer Price Index (PPI) release.

The price index for inputs to new residential construction — which combines goods and services — rose 0.3% in October and is 10.4% higher than a year ago, NAHB economist Jesse Wade said. By comparison, the PPI for final demand overall increased 0.3% in October and 6.5% year over year.

For builders, that gap underscores a persistent cost squeeze even as some headline inflation measures appear to cool.

Goods make up roughly 60% of the residential construction inputs index. Overall, the price of input goods used in new residential construction (including energy) was unchanged in October, following a 1.7% jump in September, and is up 9.8% over the past 12 months.

That stability at the top line masks diverging trends beneath the surface:

Key product categories continue to move higher:

For single-family and multifamily builders, the mix of slightly moderating year-over-year gains in some materials and still-elevated levels in others complicates bid setting, option pricing and value-engineering decisions heading into 2027 build cycles.

Service inputs to residential construction, which cover distribution margins, transportation and a range of other services, rose 0.7% in October and are 11.3% higher than October 2025, according to NAHB.

The services side of the index is split into three major components:

All three are running well above general inflation:

Because services often adjust more slowly than commodity prices, this side of the index tends to be “stickier.” For builders, that means even if some material categories ease, fully loaded installed costs can remain elevated due to freight, storage and distribution charges.

The October PPI data reinforces several themes for homebuilders, land developers and their capital partners:

Heading into 2027 selling and construction seasons, the NAHB analysis suggests that homebuilders should not assume relief in headline energy prices will translate directly into lower house costs. Instead, monitoring both material and service-side inflation — and baking higher contingencies into pro formas — will remain critical as the industry navigates persistently high input inflation alongside tighter capital markets and cautious buyers.k

#5465. JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 7, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:47 am

Firmly, a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil, Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.

Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.

The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.

Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

The company this week also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.

Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.

The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan, a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business. Firmly is based in Issaquah, Wash., and its engineering leaders work in Seattle. The company also has engineering teams in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Chennai, India.
